title: CIPHER: Contextual Instruction Precedence and Hierarchy Evaluation for Repositories

authors.name: Awaiz Ahmed

abstract: Repository instruction files such as AGENTS.md guide AI coding agents, and a nested file may legitimately refine or replace guidance from its ancestors, so an apparent disagreement is not necessarily a defect. CIPHER defines a task-conditioned classification of instruction pairs under a declared directory-precedence profile into five labels: unresolved conflict, valid override, disjoint applicability, compatible, and insufficient evidence. From a public configuration dataset we built a traceable pilot set of 27 real instruction pairs from eight repositories at pinned commits, each with a context-changing variant and an order control, and an annotation protocol for blinded labeling. Human reference labels have not yet been collected, so this short paper reports a preliminary analysis, frozen by hash before predictions were opened, that needs none: accuracy on the 26 cases whose label the profile fixes from file paths (5 mined originals, 16 constructed variants, 5 controls), and label-free measures elsewhere. With one local open-weight model, a direct prompt and a structured pipeline that computes applicability and precedence explicitly, both given the same evidence packet, were correct on all 26 profile-determined cases, whereas a keyword heuristic flagged 2 of them as conflicts. No model arm judged any original or variant to be an unresolved conflict. The arms disagreed mainly on condition-based applicability, but an exact repeat of the direct prompt changed of 81 labels, so such small differences are within run-to-run variation. The structured pipeline used more output tokens than the direct prompt (3589 versus 2177 per case) without a measurable gain.
status: Preliminary results without human labels (profile-determined subset and label-free measures)
